messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 36

# Marcus Chen: Rebuilding After the Spill

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his weathered hands folded in his lap, the calluses and permanent stains from decades of roofing work telling their own story. At sixty-six, he had planned to work another five years before retiring. That plan changed on a Tuesday morning in March when a chemical storage facility near the industrial complex where he was replacing gutters experienced a catastrophic leak.

He remembers the smell first—acrid, chemical, nothing like anything he'd encountered in forty-three years of roofing. He was on a ladder thirty feet up when the alarm started. By the time he climbed down, a yellowish cloud was drifting across the work site. The evacuation was chaotic. Marcus, along with fifteen other workers, was exposed before anyone fully understood what was happening. He spent that night in the hospital being monitored, then was released with assurances that his exposure was minimal, that he'd be fine.

But fine is not what came.

Within weeks, Marcus began experiencing symptoms he couldn't quite name. His chest felt tight constantly, as if the chemical had left something inside him that wouldn't dissolve. He started having nightmares—vivid, graphic dreams where he's back on that ladder and the cloud is consuming him, filling his lungs, suffocating him from the inside. He wakes gasping, his heart racing, his shirt soaked through. His wife, Linda, has learned not to touch him suddenly when he wakes; the startle response is too intense.

The physical symptoms compound the anxiety. Marcus experiences shortness of breath that his pulmonologist cannot fully explain. His chest tightens without warning, sending him into panic spirals where he's convinced something is terribly wrong. He's had the cardiac workup twice. His heart is fine. But the fear doesn't care about test results.

Work has become nearly impossible. Marcus has always been the type to push through discomfort—that's what roofing demands. But now, when he's up on a roof, he becomes hypervigilant about smells, about any unusual odor in the air. A few months ago, he caught the faint scent of something chemical on a commercial job and immediately descended, hands shaking, unable to continue. His boss was understanding, but Marcus felt the shame of it acutely. He's the reliable one. He's the one who shows up.

He's taken to avoiding situations where he might encounter unfamiliar smells. He no longer goes to the hardware store—the paint and solvent section triggers acute anxiety. He's stopped attending his weekly poker game with friends because the anxiety about being in an enclosed space with potential air quality concerns has become too much. Linda finds him checking the weather obsessively, worried about wind patterns that might carry pollutants, though he can't quite articulate why this matters so much.

The hypervigilance extends into his home. He's installed air purifiers in every room, spending money he hadn't budgeted for, checking them compulsively. He wakes at three in the morning sometimes, seized by the conviction that something is wrong with the air, and gets up to check the filters, to open windows, to stand outside breathing deeply until his racing heart settles.

Marcus knows, intellectually, that the exposure was brief and that he was told he's medically fine. But his body doesn't seem to believe this information. His mind replays that moment on the ladder constantly—the smell, the alarm, the panic, the cloud. He's lost weight. He's irritable with Linda in ways that frustrate him; she doesn't deserve his snapping at her over small things. He feels trapped between the life he had and a new reality where his own body has become unpredictable, where safety feels like an illusion he can no longer maintain.
